An example of the slow TV genre can be seen in *Nordlandsbanen: Minutt for Minutt*, a 2012 Norwegian show featuring an uninterrupted 10-hour real-time broadcast of a train ride from Trondheim to Bodø.
Slow TV programs provide uninterrupted broadcasts of ordinary events, such as train rides, in real time.
With their uninterrupted broadcasts, slow TV programs offer what film scholar Helen Wheatley calls the "'unspectacular' spectacle" of ordinary events occurring in real time.

questions.rationale: Only choice B names a specific program and describes it.
questions.explanation: The goal calls for one particular slow TV program, and choice B names *Nordlandsbanen: Minutt for Minutt* and fills in its year, country, length, and subject. Choice A names a book about the genre rather than a program in it. Choice C describes the genre in general and mentions train rides only as a category. Choice D quotes a scholar's characterization of the genre without naming any program at all.

questions.passageText:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes.

• Calida Garcia Rawles is an African American painter.
• She is known for her large-scale, hyperrealistic paintings depicting African American figures in water.
• The painting *Lightness of Being* (24 by 30 in) depicts a young man with his arms outstretched floating on the right side of the canvas.
• *Lost in the Shuffle* (36 by 24 in) depicts two young men with their arms outstretched floating in the bottom left and upper right corners of the canvas.
• She paints the water with vivid blue colors, including periwinkle and cobalt.
• The mood in the paintings is placid.
questions.questionText: Which choice most effectively uses information from the given sentences to emphasize the location of the figures in *Lost in the Shuffle*?

choices.text: While the number of figures may differ, constant among Rawles's hyperrealistic works is the placid mood that the paintings evoke.
In Rawles's painting *Lost in the Shuffle*, two young men are depicted in the bottom left and upper right corners of the canvas.
At 36 by 24 inches, Rawles's *Lost in the Shuffle* is even larger than the sizable 24-by-30-inch painting *Lightness of Being*.
Rawles captures the water in paintings such as *Lightness of Being* and *Lost in the Shuffle* in vivid hues of periwinkle and cobalt.

questions.rationale: Choice B states where the two figures sit on the canvas — bottom left and upper right.
questions.explanation: The goal is the placement of the figures within *Lost in the Shuffle*, and only choice B gives it. Choice A emphasizes the shared placid mood, which is about atmosphere rather than position. Choice C emphasizes canvas dimensions and compares the two paintings' sizes. Choice D emphasizes the colors of the water across both works. None of the three says where in the painting the men appear.

questions.passageText:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes.

• Jean-Michel Basquiat was an American artist who produced more than two thousand drawings and paintings.
• Most of his works were completed in New York City in the 1980s.
• His work *Mater* was completed in 1982.
• The work is composed of acrylic and oil stick on canvas and measures 72 inches by 84 inches.
• *Mater* was purchased by a private collection for 5.8 million dollars in a 2009 auction.
questions.questionText: Which choice most effectively uses information from the given sentences to emphasize the scope of Basquiat's work?

choices.text: *Mater* is just one of more than two thousand drawings and paintings completed by American artist Jean-Michel Basquiat.
Though artist Jean-Michel Basquiat completed most of his two thousand-plus drawings in the 1980s, his work *Mater* is composed of acrylic and oil stick on canvas.
At a 2009 auction, artist Jean-Michel Basquiat's *Mater*, composed of acrylic and oil stick on canvas, sold for 5.8 million dollars.
Decades after artist Jean-Michel Basquiat completed his 1982 work *Mater*, a private collection purchased it for 5.8 million dollars.

questions.rationale: "Just one of more than two thousand" puts the size of Basquiat's output in the emphatic position.
questions.explanation: Scope here means the sheer extent of the artist's output, so the sentence must foreground the two-thousand-plus figure. Choice A does, framing *Mater* as one item within that body of work. Choice B mentions the number but subordinates it to a contrast with the painting's materials, and the contrast it draws is not a real one. Choice C emphasizes the auction price and the medium. Choice D emphasizes the gap between completion and sale.
